# Connection: Background Task Exit-Code Failures Can Be False Positives

## The Connection

On 2026-07-18, the SpeedProfiling ticket-04 full-game data pull ran as a background R task that reported "failed / exit code 1," yet the task's own log showed a clean end-to-end run — the 10 Hz cache hit, 188 play-by-play plays saved, and the expected outputs written to disk (see [[concepts/speedprofiling-velocity-project]]). Exit codes and background-task status notifications are intermediate signals, not ground truth. A non-zero exit code from a detached or backgrounded process can be an artifact of the process-management layer (shell wrapper, harness notification, cleanup step) rather than a genuine failure of the work the process performed. # Connection: Set a Signal's Predicate to the Operational Question When You Build It

## Key Points

- [[connections/status-field-scope-narrower-than-the-question]] gives a rule for reading a signal: before deciding a signal lied, ask what claim it actually makes. [[concepts/automation-stack-doctor]] shows the same rule used when building a signal: change what the signal measures so that it answers the question you care about.
- On 2026-07-27, the session-end hook's timeout alarm measured "this hook missed its 45-second window." Once the hours-scale reindex moved into the nightly task, a missed window became expected and meant nothing on its own.
- Two changes fixed this without silencing the alarm. The threshold went from 3 to 6 consecutive misses, and a successful nightly reindex now resets the streak counter. After these changes, the alarm means "the nightly safety net has fallen behind," which is the question that matters.
- The cloud-check UTC bug is the reading-side failure from B, caught inside A. The freshness field's math mixed local and UTC time, and the result was read as "the backup is stale." Converting timestamps to UTC fixed the check itself, not the threshold.
- Taken together: fix scope gaps when you build a signal where possible. Read-side checks are the fallback for signals you can't change, such as `launchctl list`.

## Details

The status-field connection covers fields you don't own. `launchctl` column 2 reports only scheduled runs, and a comment counter can't tell who wrote a comment. There, the only fix is to name the field's scope when you read it, and sometimes to leave a stale red status alone until the next scheduled run clears it. The stack-doctor session handled a signal it did own. A hook alarm that fired on every slow session was accurate about its narrow claim ("this pass timed out") but useless for the real question ("is the index falling behind?"). The fix was to change the claim, not to turn the alarm off. The nightly task resets the streak, and the threshold is set so that only a failure of the safety net can trigger it.

This matters because the two articles describe opposite ends of one gap. If a signal is narrower than the question, someone pays for it: either the designer pays once, by rewiring the signal (reset-on-success, a raised threshold, UTC-normalized comparisons), or every reader pays on every alert, by working out what the field really means. When you own the signal, that interpretation can be built in, as the 2026-07-27 session did. When you don't own it, as with `launchctl` on 2026-08-31, the read-side discipline is all you have. For each new alarm, ask which question it should answer and what event would make it diverge from that question. Then wire up whatever clears it or limits it (a counter reset, a dedup, a normalization) before relying on it.

# Connection: Verify Directly, Don't Trust the Intermediate Layer

## The Connection

Both substantive sessions on 2026-04-22 ran into a version of the same problem: a tool or agent produced output that *looked* fine - a citation with a plausible author list, a photo wired into HTML with a correct relative path - but was actually wrong or unverifiable through the usual checking method. In [[concepts/the-monitor-newsletter]], Blake Wright's photo failed to appear in the localhost preview server even though the HTML and file path were both correct.

## Key Insight

In both cases, the fix was not to redo the original work but to change the *verification method* to something closer to the ground truth. The hallucinated citations were caught by extracting the actual PDF text with PyPDF2 and reading it directly, rather than trusting the agent's summarized output. The "broken" photo was confirmed to be fine by opening the HTML file directly in Chrome via `file://`, rather than trusting the brainstorm preview server's rendering. The shared lesson: when an agent, tool, or service produces output that looks plausible but can't be easily double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive, lower-level check (raw file text, direct file rendering) before accepting the result as correct.

# Global Prompt and Hook Stack Audit (2026-09-29)

On 2026-09-29 the global prompt and hook stack was audited and repaired in a single pass: nine fixes were applied and pushed across four repos, cutting per-session startup context from roughly 17 KB to 5.7 KB while removing self-contradictory and machine-specific instructions. The user gave blanket authorization for the proposed changes rather than reviewing each one, and the work closed with a handoff at `~/Desktop/DEV/docs/handoffs/2026-09-29-prompt-audit.md`. On 2026-09-30 the audit's deliberately-deferred item — the uncleared error log — was resolved once its contents had root causes.

## Key Points

- **Error log summarized by type, not occurrence.** The startup error section now emits one line per error *type* instead of one per occurrence. This single change accounts for most of the ~17 KB → ~5.7 KB startup-context reduction, and it was also what surfaced four previously invisible error types (daily-backup ×6, perch-pull ×2, compiler-backlog ×3, and an adjudication run at 315k against a 250k token budget) that the first partial-log pass had missed.
- **A hook can neutralize a plugin's injected prompt text, but must re-apply itself.** `hooks/superpowers-quiet.mjs` strips the superpowers "MUST invoke / EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT" block at each session start. Because plugin updates overwrite plugin files, the hook re-applies the strip every session; one noisy session after any plugin update is expected. All superpowers skills remain available — only the imperative prompt block is removed.
- **Bans rewritten as goals; descriptions rewritten as instructions.** Both global instruction files were reworded from prohibitions to objectives, the session routine (pull + read STATUS at start, commit + push at end) was converted from a *description* of practice into an actual instruction, and an AGENTS.md contradiction between "output nothing" and "report errors" at startup was removed.
- **Machine-specific paths now enumerate both machines everywhere.** Vault, memory-folder, and CLI paths list both the Windows and macOS values in both machine templates plus `DEV/CLAUDE.md` and `RESEARCH.md`.
- **The error log is cleared only once its contents are explained, and only after a dated copy.** On 2026-09-29 and again the morning of 2026-09-30, `transcripts/.errors.log` was deliberately left alone — 14 KB of 9/23–9/28 failures were still unfixed, and clearing would have hidden them. Once the stack-doctor pass that day attributed the memsearch timeouts to a stopped Milvus container and the 9/27 flush failure to a usage limit, the log was cleared *after* saving a dated copy, so the next startup warning shows only new failures.
- **Trimming already-tight prose yields little.** Memory-index trimming returned only 8.4 KB → 7.7 KB against an estimate of "roughly halve," because most lines were already compressed. Structural changes (summarize by type) beat line-level editing.

## Details

The audit's most transferable result is a ranking of context-reduction tactics by yield. Rewriting the error log to summarize per error *type* collapsed a repetitive, unbounded section into a bounded one and delivered the bulk of the savings; hand-trimming the memory index recovered 0.7 KB against a predicted halving because the prose was already dense. The general lesson is that per-session context bloat usually lives in *repetition* — N occurrences of the same condition rendered N times — rather than in verbosity, so the first place to look is any section whose length scales with event count instead of with distinct state.

The error-summary rewrite also had a correctness payoff independent of size. The original pass read only part of the log and therefore missed four error types entirely; the new full-log summarizer found them. A truncating summarizer is worse than no summarizer in one specific way — it produces a short, confident-looking section that silently omits whole failure classes. The `superpowers-quiet.mjs` hook establishes a pattern worth naming: a plugin that injects imperative prompt text can be muted at the consumer side without uninstalling it, by stripping the block at session start. # Windows Task Scheduler: Full Executable Path Requirement

Windows Task Scheduler spawns processes with a minimal environment that does not include the standard user PATH. Consequently, executables must be specified by their full absolute path in Task Scheduler actions — using a bare executable name (e.g., `pwsh.exe`) fails silently, with the scheduled task appearing to run but producing no actual output or effect. On 2026-06-11, this was encountered while registering KeystoneOS's morning cadence task: `pwsh.exe` failed silently until replaced with `C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe`.

## Key Points

- **Task Scheduler uses a minimal spawn environment without user PATH:** unlike an interactive terminal, Task Scheduler's process environment does not include directories added to PATH by user profile scripts, installer tools, or shell configuration. Only the system PATH (machine-level registry entries) is available.
- **Bare executable names fail silently:** `pwsh.exe`, `python.exe`, `node.exe`, `uv.exe` — any tool installed by a user-mode installer — will produce a "program not found" condition that Task Scheduler logs as a task failure without surfacing a clear error in the UI.
- **Fix: use full absolute paths.** Examples: `C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe` (PowerShell 7), `C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe` (Windows PowerShell 5.1). Obtain the correct path interactively via `(Get-Command pwsh.exe).Source`.
- **Diagnose via Last Run Result in Task Scheduler properties:** error codes like 0x1 (general failure) or 0xFFFD0000 (program not found) are visible in the task's Last Run Result field. A "0x0" success code with no observable output is the signature of the silent-failure mode where the scheduled action completed immediately without doing anything.
- **Applies to all Windows automation systems that spawn with minimal environments:** Task Scheduler, Windows Service installers, COM servers, and scheduled CI runners share this constraint — any tool not in the machine-level system PATH must be called by absolute path.

## Details

# Connection: A Verified Source Does Not License the Framing Placed On It

## The Connection

Two audits in this knowledge base reached the same structural verdict from opposite directions. On 2026-09-18, the TOS evidence brief cited real, correctly located papers and still misquoted three of them numerically, ran a Poisson cluster argument backwards, and drew causal conclusions from descriptive designs ([[concepts/tos-evidence-brief-adversarial-audit]]). On 2026-09-26, an X post cited a real, recent, code-published paper — "Just Ask Jev," arXiv 2609.29429 — and still misrepresented both its scope (a checker of *other models'* outputs) and its headline number (63× cheaper than LLM-as-judge on published benchmarks, not cheaper than the reader's own spend) ([[concepts/external-claim-audit-against-own-repo]]).

In the first case Eric was the author of the distortion; in the second he was its intended audience. The audit procedure that caught it was identical: go to the primary artifact and check what it actually measured, against what.

## Key Insight

The distortion reliably enters at the summarization boundary, and the direction of travel does not matter. A one-pager compresses a review and strips the qualifiers that constrained the claim ([[concepts/compression-amplifies-distortion]]); a promotional post compresses a paper and strips the baseline the number was measured against. Both produce an artifact that is *more quotable and less true* than its source, and in both cases the source's own legitimacy is what lends the compressed version its credibility. Checking the citation exists is therefore the cheapest and least informative verification available — it confirms the one property that was never in doubt.

The specific question that does the work is "measured against what?" A 63× cost multiple and a misquoted effect size fail the same way: the number is real somewhere, in a comparison the reader is not making. This is the cost analogue of forecast-slicing on a model's own output, where a real-looking bias is an artifact of the comparison set rather than of the thing being measured.

A practical asymmetry follows. When receiving a claim, the reader must reconstruct the source's baseline before acting — which is why the 2026-09-26 audit turned "should we adopt this?" into "we already do four of five, and the fifth doesn't apply at our volume." When *emitting* a claim, the author must propagate corrections to every derived artifact, because the compressed copies carry the distortion furthest and are the ones that get sent. One direction demands decompression; the other demands propagation.

## The Connection

# Connection: Background Task Exit-Code Failures Can Be False Positives

## The Connection

On 2026-07-18, the SpeedProfiling ticket-04 full-game data pull ran as a background R task that reported "failed / exit code 1," yet the task's own log showed a clean end-to-end run — the 10 Hz cache hit, 188 play-by-play plays saved, and the expected outputs written to disk (see [[concepts/speedprofiling-velocity-project]]). This is a specific instance of a recurring class of tooling failure documented across the environment: a status/exit signal reporting failure that does not reflect the actual outcome, where the ground truth lives in a lower-level artifact (a log file, an on-disk output) rather than the reported status code.

## Key Insight

Exit codes and background-task status notifications are intermediate signals, not ground truth. A non-zero exit code from a detached or backgrounded process can be an artifact of the process-management layer (shell wrapper, harness notification, cleanup step) rather than a genuine failure of the work the process performed. The correct diagnostic response is to inspect the actual output — the log's final lines, the files on disk, the row counts — before treating the reported failure as real. On 2026-07-18 the SpeedProfiling pull's on-disk verification (8,932,931 rows for all 61/61 athletes, 69/69 tests passing, both caches confirmed hit on re-run) established the run had actually succeeded despite the exit-1 notification.

This mirrors the memsearch silent `exit 1` failure class (2026-06-13), where a memsearch invocation exited 1 with no surviving diagnostic output — the inverse problem, where a real failure left no trace and could not be diagnosed from the status alone. Together the two cases bracket the same lesson: the exit code and the actual outcome are independent signals that must be reconciled by examining the primitive artifacts. This is the process-execution analog of the broader "verify directly, don't trust the intermediate layer" discipline: just as agent citations, preview-server renders, and retrieval scores can misrepresent ground truth, so can a process's reported exit status.

- 2026-06-13: memsearch produced a silent `exit 1` "with no surviving diagnostic output" — the complementary case where the exit code was the only signal and no artifact survived to reconcile it against (see [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]]).

# Connection: Set a Signal's Predicate to the Operational Question When You Build It

## Key Points

- [[connections/status-field-scope-narrower-than-the-question]] gives a rule for reading a signal: before deciding a signal lied, ask what claim it actually makes. [[concepts/automation-stack-doctor]] shows the same rule used when building a signal: change what the signal measures so that it answers the question you care about.
- On 2026-07-27, the session-end hook's timeout alarm measured "this hook missed its 45-second window." Once the hours-scale reindex moved into the nightly task, a missed window became expected and meant nothing on its own.
- Two changes fixed this without silencing the alarm. The threshold went from 3 to 6 consecutive misses, and a successful nightly reindex now resets the streak counter. After these changes, the alarm means "the nightly safety net has fallen behind," which is the question that matters.
- The cloud-check UTC bug is the reading-side failure from B, caught inside A. The freshness field's math mixed local and UTC time, and the result was read as "the backup is stale." Converting timestamps to UTC fixed the check itself, not the threshold.
- Taken together: fix scope gaps when you build a signal where possible. Read-side checks are the fallback for signals you can't change, such as `launchctl list`.

## Details

The status-field connection covers fields you don't own. `launchctl` column 2 reports only scheduled runs, and a comment counter can't tell who wrote a comment. There, the only fix is to name the field's scope when you read it, and sometimes to leave a stale red status alone until the next scheduled run clears it. The stack-doctor session handled a signal it did own. A hook alarm that fired on every slow session was accurate about its narrow claim ("this pass timed out") but useless for the real question ("is the index falling behind?"). The fix was to change the claim, not to turn the alarm off. The nightly task resets the streak, and the threshold is set so that only a failure of the safety net can trigger it.

This matters because the two articles describe opposite ends of one gap. If a signal is narrower than the question, someone pays for it: either the designer pays once, by rewiring the signal (reset-on-success, a raised threshold, UTC-normalized comparisons), or every reader pays on every alert, by working out what the field really means. When you own the signal, that interpretation can be built in, as the 2026-07-27 session did. When you don't own it, as with `launchctl` on 2026-08-31, the read-side discipline is all you have. For each new alarm, ask which question it should answer and what event would make it diverge from that question. Then wire up whatever clears it or limits it (a counter reset, a dedup, a normalization) before relying on it.

# Connection: Verify Directly, Don't Trust the Intermediate Layer

## The Connection

Both substantive sessions on 2026-04-22 ran into a version of the same problem: a tool or agent produced output that *looked* fine - a citation with a plausible author list, a photo wired into HTML with a correct relative path - but was actually wrong or unverifiable through the usual checking method. In [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]], a background repair agent's citation fixes for IDs 286, 287, and 358 contained hallucinated author lists despite correctly identifying the papers' topics. In [[concepts/the-monitor-newsletter]], Blake Wright's photo failed to appear in the localhost preview server even though the HTML and file path were both correct.

## Key Insight

In both cases, the fix was not to redo the original work but to change the *verification method* to something closer to the ground truth. The hallucinated citations were caught by extracting the actual PDF text with PyPDF2 and reading it directly, rather than trusting the agent's summarized output. The "broken" photo was confirmed to be fine by opening the HTML file directly in Chrome via `file://`, rather than trusting the brainstorm preview server's rendering. The shared lesson: when an agent, tool, or service produces output that looks plausible but can't be easily double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive, lower-level check (raw file text, direct file rendering) before accepting the result as correct.

# Global Prompt and Hook Stack Audit (2026-09-29)

On 2026-09-29 the global prompt and hook stack was audited and repaired in a single pass: nine fixes were applied and pushed across four repos, cutting per-session startup context from roughly 17 KB to 5.7 KB while removing self-contradictory and machine-specific instructions. The user gave blanket authorization for the proposed changes rather than reviewing each one, and the work closed with a handoff at `~/Desktop/DEV/docs/handoffs/2026-09-29-prompt-audit.md`. On 2026-09-30 the audit's deliberately-deferred item — the uncleared error log — was resolved once its contents had root causes.

## Key Points

- **Error log summarized by type, not occurrence.** The startup error section now emits one line per error *type* instead of one per occurrence. This single change accounts for most of the ~17 KB → ~5.7 KB startup-context reduction, and it was also what surfaced four previously invisible error types (daily-backup ×6, perch-pull ×2, compiler-backlog ×3, and an adjudication run at 315k against a 250k token budget) that the first partial-log pass had missed.
- **A hook can neutralize a plugin's injected prompt text, but must re-apply itself.** `hooks/superpowers-quiet.mjs` strips the superpowers "MUST invoke / EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT" block at each session start. Because plugin updates overwrite plugin files, the hook re-applies the strip every session; one noisy session after any plugin update is expected. All superpowers skills remain available — only the imperative prompt block is removed.
- **Bans rewritten as goals; descriptions rewritten as instructions.** Both global instruction files were reworded from prohibitions to objectives, the session routine (pull + read STATUS at start, commit + push at end) was converted from a *description* of practice into an actual instruction, and an AGENTS.md contradiction between "output nothing" and "report errors" at startup was removed.
- **Machine-specific paths now enumerate both machines everywhere.** Vault, memory-folder, and CLI paths list both the Windows and macOS values in both machine templates plus `DEV/CLAUDE.md` and `RESEARCH.md`.
- **The error log is cleared only once its contents are explained, and only after a dated copy.** On 2026-09-29 and again the morning of 2026-09-30, `transcripts/.errors.log` was deliberately left alone — 14 KB of 9/23–9/28 failures were still unfixed, and clearing would have hidden them. Once the stack-doctor pass that day attributed the memsearch timeouts to a stopped Milvus container and the 9/27 flush failure to a usage limit, the log was cleared *after* saving a dated copy, so the next startup warning shows only new failures.
- **Trimming already-tight prose yields little.** Memory-index trimming returned only 8.4 KB → 7.7 KB against an estimate of "roughly halve," because most lines were already compressed. Structural changes (summarize by type) beat line-level editing.

## Details

The audit's most transferable result is a ranking of context-reduction tactics by yield. Rewriting the error log to summarize per error *type* collapsed a repetitive, unbounded section into a bounded one and delivered the bulk of the savings; hand-trimming the memory index recovered 0.7 KB against a predicted halving because the prose was already dense. The general lesson is that per-session context bloat usually lives in *repetition* — N occurrences of the same condition rendered N times — rather than in verbosity, so the first place to look is any section whose length scales with event count instead of with distinct state.

The error-summary rewrite also had a correctness payoff independent of size. The original pass read only part of the log and therefore missed four error types entirely; the new full-log summarizer found them. A truncating summarizer is worse than no summarizer in one specific way — it produces a short, confident-looking section that silently omits whole failure classes. The lifecycle of that log then demonstrates the complementary discipline: a warning log is a standing work queue, so clearing it is a claim that its contents are resolved. Holding it uncleared for two sessions while the failures were unexplained, then clearing it on 2026-09-30 only after each class had a root cause (Milvus container down; a usage-limit hit) and only after archiving a dated copy, preserves both properties — the next startup warning becomes a true signal about *new* failures, and nothing is actually destroyed. The dated copy is what makes clearing reversible, and therefore safe.

The `superpowers-quiet.mjs` hook establishes a pattern worth naming: a plugin that injects imperative prompt text can be muted at the consumer side without uninstalling it, by stripping the block at session start. The cost is that the fix is not durable in the plugin's own files, so the hook must re-assert itself each session — the same install-time-capture-goes-stale problem seen elsewhere in this environment, resolved here by refusing to capture at install time at all and re-deriving the desired state every session. Verification was deliberately pushed to the *next* session start rather than asserted at the end, because the fixes only take effect on a fresh read of `settings.json`. The Mac-side item could not be automated at all — the new "paths that differ" section in `machine.macos.md` must be copied by hand into the Mac's own unsynced `machine.md`.

# Windows Task Scheduler: Full Executable Path Requirement

Windows Task Scheduler spawns processes with a minimal environment that does not include the standard user PATH. Consequently, executables must be specified by their full absolute path in Task Scheduler actions — using a bare executable name (e.g., `pwsh.exe`) fails silently, with the scheduled task appearing to run but producing no actual output or effect. On 2026-06-11, this was encountered while registering KeystoneOS's morning cadence task: `pwsh.exe` failed silently until replaced with `C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe`.

## Key Points

- **Task Scheduler uses a minimal spawn environment without user PATH:** unlike an interactive terminal, Task Scheduler's process environment does not include directories added to PATH by user profile scripts, installer tools, or shell configuration. Only the system PATH (machine-level registry entries) is available.
- **Bare executable names fail silently:** `pwsh.exe`, `python.exe`, `node.exe`, `uv.exe` — any tool installed by a user-mode installer — will produce a "program not found" condition that Task Scheduler logs as a task failure without surfacing a clear error in the UI.
- **Fix: use full absolute paths.** Examples: `C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe` (PowerShell 7), `C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe` (Windows PowerShell 5.1). Obtain the correct path interactively via `(Get-Command pwsh.exe).Source`.
- **Diagnose via Last Run Result in Task Scheduler properties:** error codes like 0x1 (general failure) or 0xFFFD0000 (program not found) are visible in the task's Last Run Result field. A "0x0" success code with no observable output is the signature of the silent-failure mode where the scheduled action completed immediately without doing anything.
- **Applies to all Windows automation systems that spawn with minimal environments:** Task Scheduler, Windows Service installers, COM servers, and scheduled CI runners share this constraint — any tool not in the machine-level system PATH must be called by absolute path.

## Details

Windows Task Scheduler runs under the SYSTEM account or a specified user account, but either way it launches processes with an environment derived from machine-level registry entries (`HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Environment`), not the richer user PATH that includes directories added by package managers (Chocolatey, Winget, Scoop), language runtimes (Python, Node, Go), or developer tool installers (uv, cargo). PowerShell 7's installation, for example, typically adds its directory to the user PATH or a machine PATH during setup, but this entry may be a user-level registry value (`HKCU\Environment`) that Task Scheduler's minimal spawn environment does not include. The practical consequence: any tool installed by a user-mode installer or whose PATH entry is a user-level registry entry rather than a machine-level one must be called by absolute path in Task Scheduler actions.

The silent failure mode is particularly confusing because the task reports successful execution in Task Scheduler's interface while producing no actual work. The distinguishing symptom is a task whose history log shows the action starting and immediately terminating with a non-zero exit code. The reliable diagnostic is to construct a minimal test action that writes a timestamp to a known file path — if the file is not updated after the task fires, the executable is not being found. Once the correct full path is confirmed via `(Get-Command pwsh.exe).Source` in an interactive terminal, that full path is substituted in the Task Scheduler action. This gotcha is an instance of the broader Windows pattern documented in [[connections/windows-process-env-fixed-at-launch]]: processes spawned by the system (hooks, schedulers, services) inherit a frozen, minimal environment at creation time that does not reflect the user's interactive shell configuration.

The Task Scheduler case is a fourth instance alongside setx propagation, hook PATH issues, and GSD bash-syntax mismatch.

# Connection: A Verified Source Does Not License the Framing Placed On It

## The Connection

Two audits in this knowledge base reached the same structural verdict from opposite directions. On 2026-09-18, the TOS evidence brief cited real, correctly located papers and still misquoted three of them numerically, ran a Poisson cluster argument backwards, and drew causal conclusions from descriptive designs ([[concepts/tos-evidence-brief-adversarial-audit]]). On 2026-09-26, an X post cited a real, recent, code-published paper — "Just Ask Jev," arXiv 2609.29429 — and still misrepresented both its scope (a checker of *other models'* outputs) and its headline number (63× cheaper than LLM-as-judge on published benchmarks, not cheaper than the reader's own spend) ([[concepts/external-claim-audit-against-own-repo]]).

In the first case Eric was the author of the distortion; in the second he was its intended audience. The audit procedure that caught it was identical: go to the primary artifact and check what it actually measured, against what.

## Key Insight

The distortion reliably enters at the summarization boundary, and the direction of travel does not matter. A one-pager compresses a review and strips the qualifiers that constrained the claim ([[concepts/compression-amplifies-distortion]]); a promotional post compresses a paper and strips the baseline the number was measured against. Both produce an artifact that is *more quotable and less true* than its source, and in both cases the source's own legitimacy is what lends the compressed version its credibility. Checking the citation exists is therefore the cheapest and least informative verification available — it confirms the one property that was never in doubt.

The specific question that does the work is "measured against what?" A 63× cost multiple and a misquoted effect size fail the same way: the number is real somewhere, in a comparison the reader is not making. This is the cost analogue of forecast-slicing on a model's own output, where a real-looking bias is an artifact of the comparison set rather than of the thing being measured.

A practical asymmetry follows. When receiving a claim, the reader must reconstruct the source's baseline before acting — which is why the 2026-09-26 audit turned "should we adopt this?" into "we already do four of five, and the fifth doesn't apply at our volume." When *emitting* a claim, the author must propagate corrections to every derived artifact, because the compressed copies carry the distortion furthest and are the ones that get sent. One direction demands decompression; the other demands propagation.

The paper tests Jev as a *checker of other models' outputs* … and the '63× cheaper' number is vs. LLM-as-judge on those benchmarks, not vs. Eric's Claude spend."

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.
